title: Meissner Effect and Josephson Radiation in Driven Dissipative Superconductors
abstract: Photo-induced superconducting signatures have been observed in several materials at temperatures far above their equilibrium critical temperatures, including magnetic field expulsion as in the Meissner effect. We propose driven-dissipative condensation of the superconducting order parameter as a mechanism for this phenomenon. In such a theory, optical pumping generates an effective gain (possibly via a parametric resonance) that overcomes the intrinsic damping of the pairing field, and stabilizes a non-equilibrium condensate whose phase rotates at an intrinsic frequency that is generally lower than, and incommensurate with, the drive frequency. We develop a phenomenological continuum theory that couples this slowly rotating order parameter to the conserved charge density and the electromagnetic gauge field. Despite its finite-frequency dynamics, the resulting state exhibits the conventional long-wavelength electromagnetic signatures of superconductivity. In three dimensions, it displays a static Meissner effect and a gapped plasmon generated by the Anderson--Higgs mechanism. In a two-dimensional sheet, it exhibits Pearl screening and the characteristic square-root plasmon dispersion. We further propose a direct experimental test based on a Josephson junction between the driven-dissipative state and an equilibrium superconductor. The junction supports an AC Josephson current at zero applied voltage and emits radiation at the intrinsic rotation frequency of the condensate. Its low, pump-dependent, and generally incommensurate frequency provides a clear signature distinguishing driven-dissipative superconductivity from equilibrium and drive-locked pairing states.
summary: This paper proposes that photo-induced superconductivity above the critical temperature arises from a driven-dissipative condensation of the superconducting order parameter. Using continuum theory, it predicts characteristic electromagnetic signatures, including both conventional Meissner effects and unique zero-bias AC Josephson radiation at an incommensurate frequency. This offers a clear experimental diagnostic to distinguish non-equilibrium pairing states.
main_problem: The paper addresses photo-induced superconducting signatures observed at temperatures above equilibrium critical temperatures, proposing a non-equilibrium mechanism to explain this phenomenon.
main_result: It predicts that the system exhibits both conventional long-wavelength superconductivity (Meissner effect, gapped plasmons in 3D) and unique zero-bias AC Josephson radiation at an intrinsic frequency ($ ar{\omega}$) distinct from the drive frequency.
method: The authors develop a phenomenological continuum theory by coupling the slowly rotating superconducting order parameter to conserved charge density and the electromagnetic gauge field.
model_or_system:
The model describes driven-dissipative condensation, where optical pumping generates gain overcoming intrinsic damping. The dynamics are governed by coupled equations for the order parameter ($\psi$) and charge density ($

key_observables: Static Meissner effect (3D), gapped plasmon dispersion (3D), Pearl screening/gapless plasmon dispersion (2D), and AC Josephson current emitting radiation at $ ar{\omega}$.
important_parameters: Intrinsic rotation frequency ($ ar{\omega}$), drive frequency ($\Omega$), dimensionality (2D vs 3D), and coupling constants derived from the continuum theory.
main_assumptions: The theory is phenomenological, assuming a slow phase rotation and relying on approximations like eliminating the amplitude mode via adiabatic approximation.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the non-equilibrium mechanism (driven-dissipative condensation) and then develops a continuum theory. It analyzes the resulting electromagnetic response in both 3D (Anderson-Higgs gap) and 2D (Pearl screening), culminating in the prediction of measurable Josephson radiation.
why_interesting: The work bridges non-equilibrium statistical mechanics with condensed matter phenomena, providing a concrete theoretical framework for understanding superconductivity driven by external fields, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems dynamics.
